lead: Low-temperature combustion (LTC) is a way to burn fuel that avoids both NOx and soot at the same time. It dilutes and premixes the charge, so the peak temperature stays below about 1900 K and the local fuel-air ratio stays lean. The price is that ignition is no longer set by a spark or an injection pulse; chemical kinetics set it. HCCI and RCCI are the two main forms. HCCI has appeared in a few production petrol engines as a lean-burn mode; RCCI so far exists only in research engines.
prereq: You need: Unit 3 (ignition delay, knock and stages of combustion), 6.1 and 6.7.

blocks.text: A conventional diesel spray burns with a diffusion flame. Inside the spray core φ is well above 1, so there is little oxygen and soot grows. Around the flame sheet the temperature is high, often above 2200 K, so NOx forms. If you add more air to cut soot, the flame gets hotter and NOx rises. If you cool the charge with EGR to cut NOx, soot rises. This is the soot-NOx trade-off.

The φ–T map plots local equivalence ratio against local temperature. φ is the equivalence ratio: actual fuel-air ratio divided by stoichiometric fuel-air ratio. Both axes are local gas properties inside the cylinder, not bulk cycle averages. The high-soot region sits on the rich side, roughly φ above 2 in the standard φ–T map, and at 1500–2500 K. The high-NOx region sits at T > about 1900 K. A window at φ below about 1 and T below about 1900 K has low values of both. LTC means any combustion strategy that keeps the burn inside this window. Two conditions are needed: the charge must be lean or well diluted, and the peak temperature must stay low. The figure shows the trade-off at a fixed rich φ: NOx climbs steeply above 1900 K while soot falls. NOx alone would be cured by cooling, and soot alone by raising temperature, so neither lever works by itself. The low-emission window needs the lean φ condition as well: only at φ below about 1 and T below about 1900 K are both low.

LTC burns cooler and leaner than a normal diesel. The heat release is spread out, and the flame, if any, is weak. The efficiency can still be diesel-like because the engine runs unthrottled and with a high compression ratio. The difficulty is ignition: a lean, cool mixture ignites slowly and unpredictably, and the burn rate is set by chemistry.

HCCI (homogeneous charge compression ignition) mixes fuel and air before compression, like a petrol engine, but ignites by compression heat, like a diesel. The charge is lean: φ is roughly 0.2–0.4. There is no spark plug and no flame front. As the piston rises, the whole charge reaches ignition conditions, and many sites ignite almost together. The burn is controlled by chemical kinetics, not by a flame speed.

blocks.where: τ is ignition delay in ms or s; A is a pre-exponential constant; E/R is the activation-temperature constant in K (about 15 000 K for diesel-like fuel); T is charge temperature in K.

blocks.text: A small rise in T shortens τ sharply. That is why HCCI needs intake air heating, hot EGR or a high compression ratio to make ignition happen, and why intake temperature control is critical.

Control knobs are intake temperature, EGR rate, variable valve timing (traps hot residual gas), compression ratio, fuel blending and stratification. None of these is a direct ignition-timing actuator like a spark or an injection pulse.

items: Gains: diesel-like efficiency from lean, unthrottled running; low pumping loss; near-zero NOx and soot.
Costs: narrow operating window; high HC and CO at low load because the charge is too cool to burn fully; very high pressure rise rate (ringing) at high load; hard cold start.

blocks.text: PCCI (premixed charge compression ignition) uses one fuel and an early direct injection. The fuel has time to mix before ignition, so the charge is partly premixed. Soot is lower than in a normal diesel because the rich core is smaller, but a φ gradient remains. Ignition timing is still set by kinetics, so PCCI shares HCCI's control problem.

RCCI (reactivity controlled compression ignition) uses two fuels with different reactivity. A low-reactivity fuel — petrol, ethanol or CNG — is port-injected to make a lean premixed charge. A high-reactivity diesel is injected later, directly into the cylinder. Ignition starts in the diesel-rich zones. The diesel then ignites the surrounding lean mixture. The reactivity gradient sets the burn rate: more diesel or a later diesel injection speeds up or delays the burn. This gives control over a wider load range and higher efficiency than HCCI.

Think of RCCI as stratification of chemistry rather than stratification of fuel alone. The port fuel sets the lean background; the direct fuel sets the ignition. It is not the same as a conventional dual-fuel engine, where a diesel pilot simply lights a gas-air mixture (see 6.7). In RCCI the two fuels are chosen for their ignition behaviour and the ratio is changed with load.

figure.caption: Local temperature decides the trade-off at a fixed rich φ: NOx climbs steeply above 1900 K while soot falls. Neither lever works by itself; the low-emission window also needs the lean φ condition. The map is a local-gas-property map, not a plot of bulk cycle peak temperature.

spec.aria: Graph of relative NOx and soot levels against local in-cylinder temperature at a fixed rich equivalence ratio; NOx climbs steeply above 1900 K while soot falls, so neither lever alone gives low emissions.

examples.question: Two HCCI runs have the same charge pressure. Run 1 has charge temperature 900 K; run 2 has 950 K. Ignition delay is τ = A exp(E/(R T)) with E/R = 15 000 K. Find τ900/τ950. State the practical meaning.
steps: Compute the reciprocal temperatures: 1/900 = 1.1111 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹; 1/950 = 1.0526 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹.
A 50 K rise cuts the delay by a factor of about 2.4. Small temperature errors change ignition timing a lot, so HCCI needs tight intake temperature control.
examples.answer: τ900/τ950 ≈ 2.4, so the 950 K run has about 2.4 times shorter ignition delay.
examples.check:
import math
ER = 15000.0
T1 = 900.0
T2 = 950.0
exponent = ER * (1.0/T1 - 1.0/T2)
ratio = math.exp(exponent)
print(round(ratio, 1))

traps: HCCI is not a spark-ignition engine running lean. There is no spark and no flame front; the whole charge auto-ignites.
LTC does not make NOx exactly zero. It keeps peak temperature below the NOx-forming range, so NOx is near zero.
Cooling alone does not kill soot. If local φ stays above 1, soot can still form; LTC needs a lean or premixed charge as well.
High-load HCCI ringing is not the same as spark knock. It is a very high pressure rise rate from fast heat release.
RCCI is not just a diesel pilot in a gas engine. The two fuels are chosen for a reactivity difference and the burn is set by that gradient.

quiz.q: What does HCCI stand for, and what ignites the charge?
quiz.a: Homogeneous charge compression ignition. Compression heat raises the whole lean charge to auto-ignition; there is no spark.

quiz.q: State the two conditions on the φ–T map that define the low-emission window.
quiz.a: Local equivalence ratio φ below about 1 (lean or diluted charge) and peak temperature below about 1900 K.

quiz.q: Why does a conventional diesel face a soot-NOx trade-off?
quiz.a: Fuel-rich spray cores make soot; high flame temperature makes NOx. More air cuts soot but raises temperature and NOx. Cooling with EGR cuts NOx but raises soot.

quiz.q: Why does HCCI need intake heating, hot EGR or a high compression ratio?
quiz.a: The lean charge is slow to auto-ignite. These measures raise charge temperature so the ignition delay becomes short enough for the piston to be near top dead centre.

quiz.q: For E/R = 15 000 K, by what factor is ignition delay shorter at 930 K than at 900 K?
quiz.a: τ900/τ930 = exp[15 000(1/900 − 1/930)] = exp(0.5376) ≈ 1.71. The delay is about 1.7 times shorter at 930 K.

quiz.q: HCCI has high HC and CO at low load but ringing at high load. Explain both from the same lean, fast-chemistry behaviour.
quiz.a: At low load the charge is too cool and too lean, so some fuel never burns: HC and CO rise. At high load the charge is richer and hotter, so many sites ignite together and heat release is very fast: pressure rise rate becomes too high.

quiz.q: Why does RCCI give a wider load range than HCCI?
quiz.a: RCCI keeps a lean port-injected background but adds a high-reactivity diesel directly. Ignition starts in diesel-rich zones and the reactivity gradient sets the burn rate. The diesel quantity and timing can be changed with load, giving direct control that HCCI lacks.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, LTC ideas appear as lean-burn modes and as part of hybrid controls; the hard part is cylinder-pressure-based closed-loop control because ignition timing drifts with temperature. Researchers study PPC (partially premixed combustion), reactivity stratification, and fuel blends. Search for “RCCI reactivity gradient”, “HCCI ringing”, “closed-loop combustion control” and “partially premixed combustion”.
